Motion: Are apostolic martyrdom and suffering good evidence for the resurrection?
Pro: Sean McDowell. Con: Paulogia (Paul Ens). Moderator: Justin Brierley.

- Assess only McDowell and Paulogia within the frozen substantive window; all exact temporal exclusions and source ownership restrictions apply. Host words are context, never attributable to either side.
- Exclude every enumerated host argument and all dependent responses, including the entire late chain approximately 1:00:08–1:08:35. Neither speaker may be credited, penalized or said to have failed to reply on the basis of that excluded chain.
- The earlier standalone Paulogia motivation proposal remains assessable as a proposal only. Do not infer McDowell failed to answer it: the later answer is excluded by scope.
- Ordinary moderator logistics, requests to define terms, and faithful recaps of an existing position introduce no independent motion argument. They are not selected moves or speaker evidence.
- McDowell explicitly limits martyrdom and suffering evidence to sincerity and an anti-conspiracy contribution within a larger resurrection case. He does not claim sincerity alone proves resurrection.
- Paulogia accepts the probable existence, sincerity and deaths of Peter and Paul; he disputes extension to the entire apostolic group and the inference from sincerity to truth. Do not convert his concession into accepting resurrection.

- Names and citations are frequently garbled: Paulogia/Paul Ens, Craig Keener, Eduard Meyer, Habermas and the several James figures. Do not silently correct exact quotations or penalize caption spelling, number, or identity errors. Any rating that needs uncertain wording requires verification.

- No independent listening or second transcript has occurred. Every selected move with uncertain material wording or attribution must be marked below high and audio verified before adjudication.
- Featured quotations must be exact complete thoughts of 3–18 words, preserving qualifications; choose a different complete passage rather than invent a completion.

The full transcript is available for context, but excluded material is not rating evidence. Both event words and temporal intervals matter: rolling captions overlap turns. moves.description: McDowell broadens martyrdom to dangerous public religious persistence connected to death, using scholarly practice and a modern priest to challenge an explicit-recantation requirement.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: McDowell gives a coherent alternative category in which persistent public proclamation under foreseeable danger can qualify as martyrdom even when no surviving source records a formal offer to recant. Principal limitation: The appeal to scholarly practice and a modern priest illustrates usage but does not establish that the ancient apostles actually satisfy the proposed definition, while the asserted breadth of agreement receives limited examination. Live burden: The pro side must connect particular people, proclamations, dangers, and deaths rather than allow a defensible definition to substitute for the historical application Paulogia requests.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: The Bulls analogy clearly illustrates the semantic point that ordinary group references can convey information about members without listing each person, and McDowell treats the inference as defeasible by contrary evidence.
